title: Stellar Nurseries
objective: After this level you can describe how stars form inside nebulae.
summary: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. The Orion Nebula, 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest big nursery.

cards.headline: Stars are being born right now, and you can see one nursery yourself.
From cloud to star
cards.body: Stars form inside cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls clumps of the cloud together. As a clump shrinks, its center gets hotter and denser, until it’s hot enough for fusion to begin. A star is born.

cards.headline: The nearest nursery
cards.body: The Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest large region of star formation. Look at the sword hanging from Orion’s belt on a dark night and you’ll see it as a fuzzy patch.

cards.fact: Hubble photographed the “Pillars of Creation” in 1995.
cards.context: These towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula are full of forming stars, one of the most famous images in astronomy.

questions.explanation: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together.

questions.prompt: What turns a shrinking clump of gas into a true star?

options.label: Its core becomes hot enough for fusion to begin
It is struck by a comet
options.rationale: Comets have no effect on this.

options.label: It cools until it freezes solid

questions.explanation: As the clump shrinks, its core heats up until hydrogen fusion ignites. Then it’s a star.

questions.prompt: From Level 36: why is infrared light so useful for studying star nurseries?

options.label: Newborn stars give off no visible light
options.rationale: They do, but dust hides it.

options.label: Nurseries are too far for visible light
options.rationale: Distance isn’t the problem; dust is.

options.label: It passes through the dust that hides forming stars

questions.explanation: Stars form inside dusty clouds that block visible light. Infrared passes through the dust, revealing them.
